items.title: Carney says he spoke with Trump in recent days, Canada ‘ready’ to strike a fair trade deal. Live updates here.
items.description: Canada and the United States expanded their trade war this week, putting new tariffs on tens of billions of dollars-worth of imported goods. Follow for live updates.
items._ogDesc: Canada and the United States expanded their trade war this week, putting new tariffs on tens of billions of dollars-worth of imported goods. Follow for live updates.
items.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he spoke with U.S. President Donald Trump in recent days. The two leaders expanded the trade war between their countries this week, putting new tariffs on tens of billions of dollars-worth of imported goods.

Trump unveiled a flurry of executive orders on Tuesday, restricting trade with Canada the same day Ottawa imposed new countermeasures against the U.S. Despite that, Carney says Canada and the U.S. are still collaborating in other areas.

Trump also recently signed an order to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” criticized Canada’s relative lower dollar, and posted a series of memes – one which called Carney “governor,” and another depicting Canada and Greenland under an American flag.

  • Carney revealed details of a plan to build millions of drones, which will in part supply Ukraine’s arsenal
  • Canada will scale back environmental review for major energy projects
  • Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is in Washington
  • Democrats call Trump’s trade offensive “pointless”

Follow for live updates:

Canada is more than the U.S.: Carney

As Carney prepares to host an investment summit in Toronto next week, he shared a message to leaders looking to invest in Canada: “We have what the world wants.”

“Canada is about so much more than being next to the United States,” he told reporters. “We’re an energy superpower, and we’re putting that into place. We have one of the largest, undeveloped resources of critical metals and minerals.”

Carney also elaborated on a list of Canada’s strengths, including its educated population, connected economy and more than a half-billion consumers that he said we’re “on track to double.”

Carney did not discourage any businesses or investors from heading to the U.S., but said Canada’s unity, reliability and respect for the rule of law makes it a good partner.

“That combination is pretty rare in the world, and it’s an attractive combination.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘We have a plan’: Carney

Speaking to reporters in Calgary, Carney said the federal government has a plan to protect Canadians and businesses as the trade war with the United States intensifies.

“Of course, there’s the situation with the U.S. The commercial discussions with the U.S.,” Carney said Thursday evening. “We have a plan. It’s the same plan from the start. We’re going to reinforce it, and the plan is to build, build here.”

Carney said the government has been “studying” the new counter-tariff measures from the Americans, but reiterated his plans to build in Canada and “diversify on an international level.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada ‘always ready to sit down’ with U.S.: Carney

When asked whether Carney planned to renegotiate the trade deal with Trump, the prime minister told reporters that Canada is “always ready to sit down in a professional way to negotiate.”

Carney did not confirm whether he had plans to negotiate before Trump’s import ban goes into effect on Sep. 29, but said the time in between will be used “to allow for companies to adjust” to the bans.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Carney can’t look into Trump’s soul

Taking questions from reporters in Calgary, Carney was asked why he feels Trump appears to be so angry with Canada.

“I can’t look deeply into the souls of others,” Carney responded, adding he speaks regularly with the president, and did so within recent days. He also said Canada is “always ready” to strike a fair deal with the U.S.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada working with U.S. despite trade war

CTV News Senior Correspondent Judy Trinh asked Carney about Canada’s ability to collaborate with the U.S. to achieve peace in Ukraine while engaged in a trade war.

“We can compartmentalize,” the prime minister responded, adding his team is in constant communication with the Americans on topics outside of trade, including Iran.

“That’s part of our responsibility,” he said.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘A matter of how long it’s going to take’: Hoekstra

United States Ambassador Pete Hoekstra told CTV News that said they don’t “refer to it as a trade war,” when asked about the ongoing tariff battle between Canada and the U.S.

Hoekstra, who is visiting Gander, N.L. to attend a Sept. 11 ceremony on Friday, claimed some Canadian politicians regretted the things they had said amid the feud.

“Let’s talk about the issue here. Let’s get (it) resolved and let’s move it forward. But now, for the next two or three days, we’re here to remember what happened 25 years ago,” he said on Thursday, referring to the quarter-century anniversary of the terror attack on New York City.

“I’m not going to get into the trade stuff here. I’ve been out of the loop now for you know four or five hours. Who knows what’s happened in the last four or five hours?” Hoesktra added.

“We’re talking about 9/11. These other things will come back. We’ll have to deal with them. They’ll get resolved. We’re going to move forward. It’s just a matter of how long it’s going to take.”

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist

Read Graham Richardson’s full story

Canada cozying up with China: Trump aide

An American economist and aide to Trump says Canada is not fighting as an equal in the ongoing trade war.

In an article published in Real Clear Markets, Peter Navarro compares Canada to a rowboat opening fire on an aircraft carrier.

“The carrier will notice. The rowboat will sink,” Navarro wrote, saying Canada is cozying up with “the mercantilist and predatory dog of Communist China” as it works to broaden its trading relationships.

“Not going to happen. Not on Trump’s watch,” he wrote. “O Canada. Make the smart move now. We’re not budging.”

Carney wants to build millions of drones

Carney says Canada will expand its drone arsenal to include millions of unmanned vehicles within the next two years. It’s part of a new plan that will combine Ukrainian battlefield experience with domestic manufacturing and AI, he said.

He made the announcement alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary, where the two leaders signed a 100-year collaboration agreement Thursday.

Carney also said Canada would establish a national drone marketplace to supply national military units with drone technology.

Under the plan, one-third of all drones manufactured in Canada will supply Ukrainian’s defence effort.

Canada’s drone arsenal presently includes about 2,000 units, said Carney.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada to join Freya project

Carney is confirming a new partnership with the EU, that will have Canada join Freya, a pan-European anti-ballistic missile defence project.

The development comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Canada and the EU were working to build a new all-encompassing alliance that will include trade, security, supply chains and critical raw materials.

Carney told reporters that Canada’s involvement will support Ukraine, but is “also indicative of Canada’s deepening relationship with European partners.”

Carney said he and the EU will “have more to say to that in Strasbourg” when he visits the European Parliament in France, next week.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘100% zoned in on the tariffs:’ Ford

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has shuffled his cabinet into what he called a “good team” to “fight the tariffs” and to “fight President Trump.”

“You’ve seen a lot of action over the last few weeks, actually, probably last month or so with President Trump, but we need a strong, strong plan to continue what we’re working on right all summer,” Ford told reporters on Thursday morning.

“Actually, and I just want to emphasize: without a break, there were no breaks, no going anywhere, I’m 100 per cent zoned in on the tariffs and on President Trump.”

Ford said he looks forward to working with the prime minister on their “strong plan” to keep moving forward, “continue prospering, continue giving people hope in Ontario, even with the tariffs coming at us.”

“We’re targeted over any jurisdiction because our manufacturing might, our technology, agricultural, financial, quite a few different areas that were the engine of Canada,” Ford said.

“So, obviously, we’re going to be targeted, but we’ll continue fighting back and making sure we have a strong, vibrant area to invest right around the world.”

Alex Arsenych, CTVNewsToroto.ca journalist

Grocers prepared for tariffs

Grocery chains are less impacted by the tariffs this time around, executives from the grocery chain Empire Co. Ltd. say.

While the grocery retailer has received some requests from suppliers to raise prices, chief customer officer Luc L’Archevêque said it hasn’t accepted any so far.

“ ... it’s too early, so we won’t accept any cost increases related to tariffs, and we’ll work very closely with our supplier partners to find solutions,” he told analysts during the company’s fiscal first-quarter earnings call on Thursday.

After last year’s tariff war, grocery chains established stronger relationships with local and non-U.S. suppliers to offer more alternatives to tariffed food items and better respond to a resurgence of the buy Canadian sentiment among shoppers.

“We have a large assortment, so customers can make many different choices to avoid U.S. products,” Empire’s chief executive Pierre St-Laurent said.

Canada could be richest country on Earth: Poilievre

Poilievre appeared on CNBC this morning to push for tariff-free trade between Canada and the U.S.

“We can be the richest country in the world,” he said during an interview, heralding Canada’s expansive coastline, potash exports, oil reserves and farmland. He also advocated for reduced taxes, shortened permitting and to “unleash free enterprise” in Canada.

Dropping tariffs, he also said, would benefit both Canada and the U.S.

“If we believe in free markets then we have to believe in free trade.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Carney meets Zelenskyy in Calgary

Carney is sitting down for a closed-door meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Calgary, Alta.

During brief remarks to reporters in the room before talks began, the prime minister reiterated Canada’s support for the country, which was invaded by Russia in February 2022.

So far, Canada has provided $26 billion in military and humanitarian support, said Carney, who pledged to provide more. He also said Canada supports Ukraine’s “path” to join NATO and the EU.

“Ukraine’s future is for Ukrainians only to decide,” he also said.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

MapQuest posts billboard with directions to Lake Ontario

MapQuest is doubling down on its decision to continue to keep Lake Ontario on its map with a six-foot billboard in Chicago.

The billboard features directions on how to get from there to Lake Ontario, with the campaign line: “It’s still Lake Ontario. And we’re still here.”

The billboard is a response to Trump’s signing of an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” last month.

Read the full story here

Brampton, Ont. unveils 10-point tariff action plan

The City of Brampton, Ont. has unveiled a 10-point plan of action in an effort to mitigate the impacts of U.S. tariffs.

Mayor Patrick Brown described it as a “practical plan to protect jobs, help businesses compete, and build a stronger local economy.”

Brown said the “economic resilience” plan will focus on three pillars: protect, protect, compete, and build.

He said the plan will entail a range of measures, including protecting local jobs, businesses and manufacturing, fostering productivity and growth, diversifying trade, attracting investment, unlocking incentives, accelerating infrastructure projects, and mobilizing cross-border support

“This action plan is about positioning our businesses to compete. This plan is about protecting jobs while building a stronger economy for tomorrow,” Brown said during a news conference late Thursday morning at Brampton City Hall.

Joanna Lavoie, CP24.com journalist

‘The time to act is now’: N.B. premier

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt says the province is taking action to support local businesses, jobs and products amid the trade war.

Announced Thursday, the series of measures aims to steer public spending toward domestic products, helping businesses diversify into new markets and provide financial support to companies feeling the impact of the latest tariffs.

“The time to act is now,” Holt told reporters.

Starting Oct. 1, the provincial government plans to prohibit the procurement of U.S. goods or services for significant contracts (estimated value over $5 million), among other measures. Find the full list here.

Melanie Price, CTVNewsAtlantic.ca journalist

Trade war impacts integrated supply chain: Michigan executive

With counter-tariffs now in effect, the ongoing feud between Canada and the U.S. is “damaging the economics” of a very integrated auto supply chain, according to a Detroit automotive executive.

“Both of our countries going back and forth is not helping something that has been built for decades and is stronger together,” Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, told CTV News channel on Thursday.

He added that the input costs are rising from both, the company and the customers’ perspectives, calling the new tariffs “above and beyond” CUSMA.

According to Stevens Jr., the consumers are going to feel the increase in prices, leading to lower demands and job cutbacks. He said they were hoping for not only a resolution, but a stronger trade agreement between the two countries.

“This really hurts companies’ inputs, and ultimately somebody has to pay for them, and that unfortunately winds up being the consumer,” he added, arguing that Canada, the U.S., and Mexico are stronger together against competition from China.

“We look at our partners and our friends literally across the river from my office here as not just trade partners, but we literally build things together and have been doing that for a long time,” Stevens Jr. said.

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist

Building ferries in B.C. would help trade battle; report

A new report says building ferries in British Columbia would help the province weather the harsh economic trade winds coming from the United States.

The report from the Centre of Future Work says building ferries in local shipyards rather than purchasing them from foreign ones would help the provincial and Canadian economy grapple with steep American tariffs.

A coalition of unions and industry leaders commissioned the report, which appears 15 months after BC Ferries announced it had contracted a shipyard owned by the Chinese government to build four major vessels at a cost that’s yet to be disclosed.

The ferry operator, which is overseen by the B.C. Ferry Authority, said at the time that no Canadian company had submitted a proposal and the winning bid from China Merchants Weihai Shipyards was at least $1 billion cheaper than others.

The Canadian Press, Read the full article here

Carney playing ‘cool’ to Trump: Mulcair

A former NDP leader says Carney’s “muted response” to Trump’s actions over the last day is a “wise” move.

Tom Mulcair told CTV News Channel on Thursday that Canada has “entered a twilight zone with Trump.”

“This is no longer chaos, this is insanity,” he described of Trump’s announcement to award $5,000 to individuals if he won in the upcoming elections.

Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre can lend a strong Conservative voice if he is more “statesman-like” instead of “trying to make it partisan,” Mulcair added.

“We do want to integrate our economies, but not at the expense of being beholden to the United States the way they tried to,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trade deal ‘would have destroyed our economy’: Ford

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says Carney was right to walk away from an “absolutely terrible deal” with the U.S. that “would have destroyed our economy from top to bottom.”

Ford made the comment during a speech at the Toronto Region Board of Trade on Thursday, where he also announced expanded eligibility for a $1-billion tariff relief program for impacted businesses and workers in Ontario.

“It was a deal that would have hurt Canadian workers, undermined Canadian sovereignty and caused permanent damage to Canadian businesses that employ hundreds of thousands of workers across our country and province,” Ford said.

He added he supports Carney’s decision to respond to the latest U.S. tariffs with “dollar-for-dollar” counter-tariffs but warned “we have to be prepared to withstand the pain” that comes with showing Trump “Canada will stand up for itself.”

“If you don’t stand up for a bully they will continue to bully,” he said.

Chris Fox, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist

Effect of U.S. motorcycle ban?

A Quebec manufacturer says the U.S. ban on Canadian motorcycles will have a “limited” impact on the upcoming fiscal year.

Moto Canada president and CEO Landon French told CTV Your Morning on Thursday that the “vast majority of production and shipments for the current season are completed.”

However, French says the current trade war has the potential to “cost jobs,” decrease product choice and increase prices. It could also make it more difficult for dealerships to supply custom-made inventory.

“Eventually we need a deal,” he said.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump’s Canada-bashing echoed at U.S. convention

Thousands of U.S. President Donald Trump’s most ardent followers have gathered in Dallas for “Trump-a-Palooza” this week and many are parroting the president’s constant bashing of Canada.

Lona Heins from Tennessee says Canada is now “communist” and no longer shares the same values as the United States.

Heins says she needs more information about bilateral trade tensions, which were escalated by the Trump administration on Tuesday, but hopes the situation can be resolved.

The Canadian Press, Read the full story here

Trump pledges US$5,000 payments if GOP wins

Trump pledged Wednesday to send every American adult US$5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, an extraordinary gambit to reverse his party’s sagging fortunes in November.

The dubious promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.

“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.”

Within an hour, Vice President JD Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump’s proposal -- at least in part -- by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy. Vance suggested it could be paid for by U.S. tariff revenues, though the suggested payment dwarfs what the U.S. has taken in through the protectionist measures.

The Associated Press

Here’s what happened on Sept. 9, 2026:

Canada scales back energy project reviews

The federal government is scaling back a major Trudeau-era environmental review process, removing several energy projects from the federal impact assessment regime and shifting responsibility for their review to the Canada Energy Regulator (CER).

The federal government said the change will “simplify the project decision process” by relying on a single federal regulator.

“Industry stakeholders expressed strong support for the proposal to have all pipeline projects reviewed exclusively by the CER. Industry actors view this as a key step toward improving regulatory certainty, reducing duplication, and streamlining approvals,” the federal government said in its regulatory impact analysis.

The move comes just as Carney gets set to lead the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto next week. It is the federal government’s attempt to attract major infrastructure investments in Canada with a goal of $1 trillion in new investment over the next five years.

Graham Richardson, CTV News Ottawa Bureau chief. Read the full story here.

Canada in ‘strong fiscal position’: finance minister

Speaking at the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne appeared confident that Canada would weather the storm from the U.S. trade war as it builds partnerships around the world.

“I see a golden opportunity in front of us,” he said. “The world is changing. America is changing. The world energy architecture is changing, and in that new world … Canada can be at the centre. Why? Because we provide stability, predictability, and trust.”

Champagne also discussed Alberta projects, Canada’s global partnerships and his efforts to help affordability for Canadians.

“We have strong fiscal position to support people,” he said. “That’s the package announced: $7.5 billion, making sure that we can provide liquidity quickly to small- and medium-sized businesses, and at the same time support affected workers.”

Elianna Lev, CTVNews.ca multi-platform writer

Canada ‘dying’ to make a deal: Trump

Trump said Canada wants to make a deal with the United States while delivering his keynote address at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas Wednesday night.

During his speech, Trump brought up his administration’s decision to rename bodies of water, which include changing Lake Ontario to “Lake America” and the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

“Lake Ontario, we’re now going to call that Lake America,” Trump said. “Canada very much wants to make a deal, they’re dying to make a deal. But it’s going to be called Lake America.”

Trump then brought up his suggestion to change the name of New Mexico, a Democrat-led U.S. state, to “New America.”

Hunter Crowther, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump’s ‘pointless’ trade war: Democrat senators

U.S. Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons, Patty Murray, Amy Klobuchar and Elissa Slotkin say in a joint statement that the states they represent rely on Canada as a key trading partner.

They say Trump is doubling down on a “pointless” trade war.

“His tariffs will squeeze our states’ small businesses harder and drive costs up for working families,” they say. “President Trump’s tariffs have already cost American families as much as $5,000 in some states, and his senseless trade war with Canada will only grow that number.”

The senators say partners around the world, including Canada, are increasingly looking to diversify away from the United States and deepen trade ties with other countries, including China.

“Congressional Republicans need to stand up to the president and do their part to give families and businesses on both sides of the border relief from this insanity,” says the statement.

Greer gave LeBlanc notice of Trump’s orders: source

According to a source close to the trade discussions, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc was given a short heads up from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer before Trump’s executive orders were made public last night.

The source tells CTV News it was a short “cordial” text exchange via messages, however, LeBlanc and Greer did not speak over the phone.

Mike Le Couteur, CTV News senior political correspondent

Poilievre heads to U.S. to promote Canada

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is heading to New York and will participate in ceremonies commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks Friday, according to a senior Conservative source.

According to the source, the trip is being carried out with the blessing of the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). Poilievre wanted to go to the United States earlier, but the PMO advised at the time such a visit would be unhelpful.

CTV News reached out to the PMO for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

Abigail Bimman, CTV News correspondent. Read the full story here.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s telecommunications regulator is implementing new rules that it says will help consumers understand information about speeds and prices when shopping for home internet plans.
items.body:
Canada’s telecommunications regulator is implementing new rules that it says will help consumers understand information about speeds and prices when shopping for home internet plans.

The CRTC’s policy, which takes effect next March, will require internet providers to advertise typical speeds associated with a plan from 7 p.m. to 11 p.m. local time on weekdays, rather than “up to” speeds that may not reflect those hours of peak usage.

The rules also mandate that providers list the monthly price after any promotion ends, which the regulator says will improve Canadians’ ability to choose a plan that fits their needs and avoid surprises.

These new disclosures, to be listed through a standardized label, were proposed by the CRTC last year. It had compared the concept to food nutrition labels at grocery stores, which list information about serving size and calories in a standardized format.

Some providers had argued it would be overly costly and redundant to provide that information as proposed, while other stakeholders said the label would help cut through promotional language and boost consumer literacy when comparing plans.

The measure is the latest in a series of consumer protections rolled out by the regulator, including its ban on activation, cancellation and modification fees that came into effect in June, plus new rules that give consumers self-serve options to adjust their plans and require service providers to notify customers when a discount on their bill is about to expire.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Mark Carney and Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed multiple declarations and initiatives on Thursday, including a 100-year partnership declaration and drone collaboration, during Zelenskyy’s official visit to Canada.
items.body:
CALGARY – Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed multiple declarations and initiatives on Thursday, including a 100-year partnership declaration and drone collaboration, during Zelenskyy’s official visit to Canada.

“This is a relationship that has flourished over 100 years, and it will flourish in the century ahead, long after this war ends,” Carney said during a joint press conference in Calgary.

According to a press release, the 100-year partnership – with framework still to come – sets out the “intention to elevate the relationship between their countries into a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and confirming their aligned nature.”

Both countries also signed a joint declaration on defence and security co-operation, along with a commitment to work together on critical minerals.

“I’m happy that we signed some very important documents. It’s not just documents, not papers. These documents mean the results, what we can have in our partnership,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

Carney, meanwhile, reaffirmed Canada’s commitment to provide additional military help to address Ukraine’s need for air defence systems and equipment by supporting Project Freya, Ukraine’s pan-European effort tfo develop a lower-cost, high-volume interceptor capable of countering Russian ballistic missile attacks.

In the past few weeks, Russia has escalated its attacks on civilian installations in Kyiv. Zelenskyy has asked NATO allies, such Norway and the United Kingdom, for more air defence weapons such as drones and missiles.

Since Russia began its war in 2022, Canada has provided $8.5 billion in military support to Ukraine, along with $750 million to help with that country’s recovery and reconstruction efforts. Canada has also imposed over 3,500 sanctions against Russia.

Earlier on Thursday, Carney also announced Canada is launching a national drone marketplace for the Canadian Armed Forces that will give Canada the capacity to produce millions of drones within the next two years.

He says Ukrainian drone companies that are world leaders will partner with Canadian companies to develop these drones, while Ukraine will benefit from Canadian skills in manufacturing and artificial intelligence.

Zelenskyy to address Liberal cabinet

Following his stop in Calgary, Zelenskyy will travel to Banff, Alta., with Carney in a joint motorcade to address the Liberal government’s cabinet planning forum on Thursday, which convenes cabinet ministers and secretaries of state to assess the progress and future plans of the federal government.

Zelenskyy landed in Calgary on Wednesday evening amid a cloak of secrecy, but the planning for his visit to address cabinet has been in the works for months.

A senior source in the Prime Minister’s Office tells CTV News that Carney extended the invitation to Zelenskyy to speak to his inner circle in June during the G7 Summit in Évian-Les-Bains, France.

Zelenskyy will address cabinet at a time when the prime minister is pursuing stronger ties with the European Union.

Carney has been invited to address European Parliament in Strasbourg, France next week. Canada is also the first non-European member of the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program, a €150-billion (approximately C$240.8-billion) defence financing and joint procurement initiative. Canada has also been selected as the headquarters for the new Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, created to finance defence projects for NATO members and allied countries.

According to the PMO source, Zelenskyy’s agenda in Canada was kept under wraps at the request of Ukraine.

Prior to his arrival in Canada, two Russian drones crossed into Moldovan airspace, where Zelenskyy’s plane was waiting to depart for Norway to attend the funeral of King Harald V.

Zelenskyy is scheduled to travel to Toronto and North Bay, Ont., before he departs Canada on Friday.

With files from The Canadian Press

TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index fell 400 points on Thursday, while U.S. markets also lost ground and the price of oil topped US$100 per barrel.

The October crude oil contract was up US$6.43 at US$102.48 per barrel.

  • Real-time TSX market updates here

The S&P/TSX composite index was down 400.28 points at 35,506.28.

In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 316.56 points at 52,064.10. The S&P 500 index was down 44.66 points at 7,591.70, while the Nasdaq composite was down 171.62 points at 26,081.72.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The Canadian dollar traded for 72.35 cents US compared with 72.47 cents US on Wednesday.

The December gold contract was down US$53.40 at US$4,407.30 an ounce.

items.body:
This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received.

VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Sept. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Western Pacific Trust Company (“WPTC”) is pleased to announce that its Board of Directors has declared its fourth consecutive annual dividend on common shares. The dividend reflects WPTC’s continued financial strength and the Board’s confidence in the Company’s long-term outlook.

The declaration follows another year of solid performance and continued progress across WPTC’s core business. Despite ongoing economic and market uncertainty, the Company has remained focused on providing responsive, specialized trust services to its clients while maintaining a strong and stable financial position.

“We are pleased to declare our fourth consecutive annual dividend on common shares,” said Alison Alfer, President & CEO. “The dividend reflects the strength and stability of WPTC’s business and our confidence in the Company’s long-term strategy. We remain focused on disciplined growth, maintaining a strong financial foundation, and delivering sustainable value to our shareholders.”

A dividend of $0.005 per common share will be payable on October 16, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on October 1, 2026.

VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Sept. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Apollo Silver Corp. (“Apollo” or the “Company”) (TSX.V:APGO, OTCQB:APGOF, Frankfurt:6ZF) reports that Ejido Benito Juárez (the “Ejido”), located in Buenaventura Municipality, Chihuahua, Mexico, has scheduled a community assembly at which members of the Ejido are expected to vote on lifting the moratorium on mineral exploration and development affecting lands which include the Cinco de Mayo project (the “Project”), which is optioned by the Company, as well as the acceptance of a long-term access agreement. The moratorium, which has been in place since 2012, represents a key outstanding condition for advancement of the Project.

The assembly is expected to take place on September 20, 2026, in accordance with the Ejido’s established governance procedures.

“We are encouraged by the progress of this process and by the strength of the relationships we have built at the community level,” said Colin Sutherland, President and Chief Executive Officer of Apollo. ”The Company respects the autonomy of the Ejido and its decision-making processes, and we look forward to continuing an open, transparent and constructive dialogue with local stakeholders.”

This upcoming assembly represents a pivotal milestone for the Project. It will be the first time since the Ejido imposed its moratorium in 2012, more than a decade ago, that the community will get to vote on rescinding the ban and re-opening the path to exploration and development at Cinco de Mayo. A vote in favour of the proposed long-term access agreement would resolve the single largest impediment to advancing the Project and would represent a defining moment in the Company’s efforts to unlock the full potential of one of the largest undeveloped silver resources in the Americas.

The Company is not a participant in the assembly or its voting process, and respects that this is a matter for the community to decide. The Company’s future activities will continue to be guided by the results of the vote, together with applicable regulatory approvals and its ongoing engagement with the community.

Cinco de Mayo is an approximate 25,000-hectare property located in the north central part of Chihuahua State, Mexico, approximately 190 kilometres northwest of the state capital of Chihuahua City in the Buenaventura Municipality. The Project is prospective for and hosts carbonate replacement type deposits including the Upper Manto Pb-Zn-Ag (Au) deposit, which consists of two parallel and overlapping manto deposits referred to as the Jose Manto and the Bridge Zone. An independent technical report and Mineral Resource estimate (“MRE”) on the Upper Manto deposit was prepared in 2012 by Roscoe Postle Associates Inc. (“RPA”). At a NSR cut-off of US$100/t, Inferred MRE was estimated to total 12.45 million tonnes at 132 grams per tonne silver, 2.86 per cent lead and 6.47 per cent zinc and 0.24 gram per tonne gold (See Apollo’s news release dated March 7, 2025). The Company’s initial review of historical data suggests that the Pegaso Zone could indicate a larger and higher-grade resource at depth.

This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received.

TORONTO, Sept. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) --  Solitaire x Alex Armen, a Toronto-based bespoke jewellery studio specializing in custom engagement rings and private commissions, has released its 2027 Canadian Engagement Ring & Jewellery Trends Report, based on an analysis of client enquiries, design consultations, and calendar bookings spanning more than eighteen months. The findings reveal Canadian consumers are increasingly moving away from mass-produced jewellery in favour of highly personalized pieces that reflect individual style, sentiment, and long-term value.

“People are no longer looking for a standard ring from a display case,” says Alex Armen, designer at Solitaire x Alex Armen. “They want a piece that reflects who they are, what they believe in, and what their relationship means to them. Jewellery is becoming more personal than ever.”

Trend #1: Yellow Gold Continues to Dominate

One of the clearest findings in the report is the continued rise of yellow gold.

While white gold and platinum remain important categories, yellow gold was the most frequently requested metal across bridal and fine-jewellery commissions. Clients consistently cited its warmth, timelessness, and heirloom quality as major factors influencing their decisions. Requests ranged from classic solitaires and elongated diamond engagement rings to gemstone-centred designs and custom wedding bands.

Trend #2: Lab-Grown Diamonds Have Become Mainstream

Lab-grown diamonds remain highly popular among younger buyers seeking larger centre stones while maintaining budget flexibility. Several enquiries focused on lab-grown diamonds between three and four carats, particularly in classic engagement ring styles.

Trend #3: Coloured Gemstones Are Moving Into the Mainstream

The report identifies coloured gemstones as one of the fastest-growing categories in custom jewellery.

Recent enquiries included alexandrite, ruby, emerald, sapphire, Paraiba tourmaline, morganite, coloured diamonds, and alternative colourless gemstones. Increasingly, clients are selecting centre stones based on symbolism, rarity, individuality, and personal connection rather than tradition alone.

Among these, alexandrite emerged as a particularly noteworthy category, reflecting growing consumer interest in unique gemstones that offer both rarity and visual intrigue.

Trend #4: Natural Diamonds Remain the Premium Choice

Despite the growth of lab-grown diamonds, natural diamonds continue to attract clients prioritizing rarity, long-term symbolism, and heirloom value.

Natural-diamond buyers frequently place greater emphasis on provenance, exceptional cut quality, and the uniqueness associated with a stone formed billions of years ago. Rather than replacing one another, natural and lab-grown diamonds appear to be serving distinct client priorities.

Trend #5: Personalisation Has Become the New Luxury

The strongest theme across all categories was the growing desire for personalization.

Rather than purchasing existing designs, clients increasingly arrived with highly specific requests that reflected their own stories, aesthetics, and relationships.

The report suggests that individuality is replacing trend-following as the primary driver behind luxury jewellery purchases.

Trend #6: Matching Wedding Bands Are Being Planned Earlier

Many couples are choosing to design engagement rings and wedding bands simultaneously to ensure proper fit and visual harmony. Requests for matching men’s and women’s bands, coordinated design language, and future wedding-band planning appeared consistently throughout the reviewed enquiries.

As consumers increasingly use conversational search platforms to research engagement rings, gemstones, jewellery design, and luxury purchases, AI is emerging as a meaningful driver of discovery within the jewellery industry.

items.title: Oil prices leap to their highest since May and drag Wall Street lower
items.description: Oil prices keep climbing to their highest levels since before the summer as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Specialists Dilip Patel works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Yuki Iwamura</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Oil prices keep climbing to their highest levels since before the summer as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Oil prices keep climbing as the war with Iran keeps clogging the global flow of crude, and they leaped Thursday to their highest levels since before the summer. That worsened worries about inflation and cranked up pressure within the bond market, helping to send stocks lower again on Wall Street.

The S&P 500 fell 0.6 per cent for a fourth straight loss, its longest such streak since June, though it’s not far from its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent.

Stocks sank under the weight of rising oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, climbed another 6.3 per cent and briefly topped US$108 per barrel for the first time since May before settling at US$107.63.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

It’s jumped from less than US$72 in early July as hopes fade that the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East anytime soon. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that oil prices likely won’t come down until after the U.S. midterm elections in November.

The jump has vaulted the price for a gallon of regular gasoline to an average of nearly US$4.28 across the United States, according to AAA. That’s up nearly 34 per cent from a year earlier and is not only costing people more at the pump but also through higher prices for all kinds of products that move by truck to store shelves.

A report on Thursday said inflation at the U.S. wholesale level accelerated to 5.4 per cent last month from 4.8 per cent in July, and retailers could eventually pass such increases in prices onto shoppers. A report is coming on Friday that will show how much inflation U.S. consumers are feeling.

The typical move to rein in high inflation is for the Federal Reserve to raise its main interest rate, the federal funds rate. Such a move then filters out through the rest of the bond market, makes it more expensive for U.S. households and businesses to borrow money, slows the overall economy and undercuts prices for investments. That hopefully would remove some of inflation’s fuel.

A report on Thursday suggested the U.S. job market may remain solid, with fewer workers applying for unemployment benefits last week. That could give the Fed more confidence that the economy could withstand higher interest rates.

Following Thursday’s reports, traders see a roughly 73 per cent chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its meeting next week. That’s up from the 61 per cent probability seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That’s also despite Trump’s consistent lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher.

The Fed’s counterpart in Europe, the European Central Bank, raised its own interest rates on Thursday in hopes of getting inflation in check. It cited “the conflict in the Middle East” and how it “continues to generate inflation pressures.”

It all pushed the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95 per cent from 4.83 per cent late Wednesday, which is a significant move for the bond market.

It’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began and is back to where it was in the autumn of 2023. That was after the Fed cranked the federal funds rate higher to get super-high inflation coming out of the COVID pandemic under better control.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

Higher yields mean investors can make more money putting their money into bonds, which can in turn make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments that are riskier than bonds.

Some investors see a 5 per cent yield on the 10-year Treasury as the next potential flashpoint. But strategists at Bank of America’s Research Investment Committee suggest 7 per cent may be the more important threshold, pointing to peaks for expensive stocks around that point in the past.

In the meantime, the rising 10-year Treasury yield is making mortgages more expensive and hurting the housing industry. One report on Thursday said the average long-term U.S. mortgage rate hit its highest level in over 14 months, while a second one said sales of previously occupied U.S. homes fell in August to their slowest pace in more than a year.

That helped sent stocks of homebuilders lower, including drops of 3.5 per cent for Lennar and 2.4 per cent for D.R. Horton.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, Macy’s fell 4.7 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. While raising its forecast for earnings this fiscal year, it warned that “there are macroeconomic and geopolitical factors that could influence” how much its customers feel comfortable spending.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Macy’s said it received US$116 million in tariff refunds from the government — US$98 million during the quarter and another US$18 million after the quarter ended. Macy’s CEO Tony Spring told The Associated Press Thursday that it’s using some of the proceeds to lower prices on certain items like furniture and other big-ticket purchases.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 44.66 points to 7,591.70. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 316.56 to 52,064.10, and the Nasdaq composite sank 171.62 to 26,081.72.

In stock markets abroad, indexes slipped across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Anne D’Innocenzio and Elaine Kurtenbach contributed to this report.

items._ogDesc: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says Canadian politicians need to tone down their rhetoric as Ottawa and Washington remain locked in a bitter trade dispute but declined to say whether U.S. President Donald Trump should do the same.
items.body:
OTTAWA — U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says Canadian politicians need to tone down their rhetoric as Ottawa and Washington remain locked in a bitter trade dispute but declined to say whether U.S. President Donald Trump should do the same.

Speaking to CTV News after arriving in Gander, N.L., for a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, Hoekstra said it was “time to take the tenor down.”

“There have been things said by Canadian politicians that, at least I’ve heard, they regret saying,” Hoekstra said. “Let’s talk about the issue here. Let’s get it resolved and move forward.”

Asked directly whether he would deliver the same message to Trump, whose social media posts have repeatedly targeted Canada and suggested the United States should absorb its northern neighbour, Hoekstra declined to answer, saying he was in Gander to commemorate Sept. 11.

The comments came as Prime Minister Mark Carney, during a press conference in Calgary, said that he remains in regular contact with Trump despite tensions between the two countries.

The trade conflict has strained bilateral relations and sparked public disputes over the deterioration of the relationship, while Trump and the White House have repeatedly mocked Canada and Carney through AI-generated memes.

“We continue to have work with the United States. We can compartmentalize across this,” Carney said after signing multiple declarations with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Thursday.

“President Trump and I remain in regular contact. I’ve spoken to him a couple of times in the last few days about issues here at home, developments in Iran and other global matters. Part of our responsibility is to work together.”

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate affordability saw a historic correction in Q2 2026. However, BMO warns home prices need further declines to normalize.
items.body:
Canadian real estate affordability continued to improve in Q2 2026, but remains far from affordable. The Bank of Canada’s (BoC) Housing Affordability Index logged an 11th straight quarter of improvement, as falling prices, lower rates, and rising incomes drove a historic correction. Unfortunately, housing remains unaffordable for most households, and affordability is still significantly worse than pre-2020. Further improvements are likely needed to revive the market, and one of Canada’s biggest banks sees only one way forward.

Bank of Canada Affordability Index

The BoC’s housing affordability index measures the share of income needed to own a home. Income is the disposable income of an average household, which skews higher than the median, thus overstating affordability. Housing costs here are defined as mortgage payments and utilities, and the index uses a 6-month rolling average of resale prices. The reading is the share of income required to make those payments, meaning higher numbers indicate housing is less affordable.

Canadian Housing Affordability Improves, but Still Not Affordable

The Bank of Canada Housing Affordability Index: Share of disposable household income needed for monthly mortgage and utility payments.

Source: Bank of Canada; Better Dwelling.

The affordability index fell 0.8 percentage points (ppts) to 41.3% in Q2 2026, shedding 2.4 ppts over the past year. Affordability has actually improved 13.2 ppts since the recent peak of 54.5% in Q3 2023, but that’s still one of the worst levels in history. Requiring more than two-fifths of income means most households still couldn’t qualify for a mortgage at the national level.

Even with one of the sharpest improvements on record, the market has a long way to go. Canadians considered it challenging to buy a home pre-2020, and the current level is still 4.9 ppts above the 36.4% reported in Q4 2019. Then there’s the issue of how affordability has improved, which caught the eye of bank economists.

Canadian Home Prices Only Have One Path Forward

In a research note to investors this morning, BMO Capital Markets warned that real estate remains rocky. “A fundamental reason why we remain cautious on the Canadian housing outlook—beyond all the distracting trade headlines—is that affordability is just not yet back to normal,” explains BMO chief economist Douglas Porter.

They note those improvements reflect the 2024/2025 rate cuts, a 20% drop in national home prices from the 2022 peak, and real personal income growth. However, they warn that it’s still a long way back to “affordable.” While anything is possible, they only really see one way forward with the current setup.

“How can it get back to ‘normal’? Incomes could grow, but that takes time. Prices could fall further, or at least dip versus income growth. And, finally, interest rates could come down a bit more—but that certainly does not seem to be in the cards, given the Bank’s hawkish stance. Thus, the burden still seems to be on prices,” explains Porter.

If you’re only following the national numbers, that may sound close to impossible. However, the sharp declines in the national numbers are skewed due to how the index basket is built. B.C. and Ontario—though still not affordable—represent the only provinces that have seen significant declines. Most provinces have seen prices grow over the past few years, and remain near all-time highs—if not currently at those levels. With valuations still very much stretched, it wouldn’t be entirely surprising to see further price declines.

items.title: Metro Vancouver condo construction hits 15-year low: CMHC
items.description: Large concentrations of unsold inventory has built up in Surrey, Vancouver and Burnaby
items._ogDesc: Large concentrations of unsold inventory has built up in Surrey, Vancouver and Burnaby
items.body:
Metro Vancouver is seeing its weakest pace of new condo construction since 2011, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

New condo construction in Metro Vancouver fell 40 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, making it the weakest first half for condo construction in 15 years, according to CMHC’s Fall 2026 Housing Supply Report released Thursday.

The continued decline in condo starts could lead to fewer completions in the future, adding pressure on available ownership housing and posing a risk to affordability in the future, said the organization.

“The condo market remains constrained by weak presales, high construction costs and growing inventories of completed and unsold units,” said the report.

Purpose-built rental apartments account for most new constructions in the region, at about 60 per cent, up from about 20 per cent a decade ago.

Rental units under construction rose about 36 per cent from 2025, as more developers favour rental projects supported by “rental-focused policies and financing,” while residential projects “have struggled to sell in recent years,” according to CMHC.

These supports include municipal incentives, rental-specific zoning policies, development charge relief and favourable financing programs designed to help maintain rental project viability, noted the report.

“Developers continue to favour rental projects because they carry less risk than condominium developments under current market conditions,” said CMHC.

“The shift appears likely to continue ... Vancouver is positioned to see several more years of strong rental completions, which could continue easing pressure in the rental market.”

But the condo market remains constrained, with large concentrations of unsold inventory have emerged in Surrey, Vancouver and Burnaby. Burnaby is seeing particularly strong inventory growth, according to the report.

With condo construction at current levels, CMHC warns that future buyers could face increased competition for a limited supply of ownership housing, which could put upward pressure on prices.

“Condominiums have traditionally been Vancouver’s primary source of new ownership housing,” said CMHC.

“Vancouver’s current pace of starts is still 5,000 to 7,000 units below what’s needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability levels by 2036.”

items.title: Vancouver commercial investment falls in cautious H1 2026
items.description: Retail posted the only gains as investors shifted toward income-producing assets
items.content: <p>Retail posted the only gains as investors shifted toward income-producing assets</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639246526073222438.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Retail posted the only gains as investors shifted toward income-producing assets
items.body:
Vancouver's commercial real estate market posted a contraction in the first half of 2026, with total investment volume declining 23% year-over-year to $3.5 billion. Capital shifted toward defensive, income-oriented strategies, according to data from Colliers and Altus Group.

The pullback extended across most major property sectors, shaped by trade policy uncertainty, moderating population inflows, softening consumer demand, and elevated financing costs.

The Bank of Canada (BoC) held its overnight rate steady at 2.25% for a fifth consecutive decision, which helped anchor long-term cost-of-capital expectations without easing underwriting pressure on buyers.

The implications of the Bank of Canada's rate hold for Canada's commercial market continued to weigh on acquisition strategies through the second quarter, with investors prioritising capital preservation over growth-oriented deployment.

Retail leads as office and industrial retreat

Retail was the only major sector to record year-over-year growth, rising a marginal 1% to $866 million.

Activity concentrated in grocery-anchored strip centres, prime street-front assets, and commercial podiums in Vancouver's urban mixed-use developments — formats offering consistent pedestrian traffic and resilient service-sector tenants, including daily-needs retailers, medical practices, and food and beverage operators. 

Office investment totalled approximately $394 million, down 46% year-over-year, constrained primarily by limited high-quality supply rather than a material decline in occupier demand.

According to Altus Group's Canadian Office Market Update, Vancouver's office availability rate reached 12.4%, up 10 basis points year-over-year and within the 12% to 13% range for a third consecutive year.

A pronounced flight to quality defined leasing activity. Class A transactions accounted for 70 deals and more than 1.3 million square feet, while Class B space drew just 16 transactions totalling approximately 245,000 square feet.

Industrial investment declined 19% year-over-year to nearly $669 million, though underlying fundamentals remained structurally tight.

Altus Group's Canadian Industrial Market Update placed Vancouver's availability rate at 5.9%, down 30 basis points year-over-year, with four consecutive quarters of positive absorption reinforcing the sector's scarcity value.

The active construction pipeline narrowed to 27 buildings totalling approximately 2.5 million square feet, roughly 51% available for lease, as developers shifted toward stricter pre-leasing requirements to manage elevated construction and financing costs.

Multi-family and land investment pull back

Multi-family transaction volume fell 41% year-over-year to nearly $372 million as investors recalibrated to softer rental growth expectations, elevated condominium inventory, and mandatory rent stabilization policies. Activity concentrated in stabilized low-rise assets and specialized care facilities.

Land investment totalled $1.2 billion for the half, down 14% year-over-year. Residential land volume declined 6% to nearly $426 million, while the industrial, commercial, and institutional sub-sector fell 18% to approximately $788 million.

Buyers continued to favour transit-oriented sites with established regulatory pathways, notably within the Broadway Plan corridor and Vancouver's Citywide Official Development Plan growth hubs.

items.title: $618K Condo Vs. $1.29M House: Inside The GTA’s August Resale Market
items.description:
The GTA’s average resale price was $993,410 in August. For a household deciding what to buy, the more useful numbers were $617,593 for a condominium apartment, and $1,288,669 for a detached home.

That is a $671,076 gap between the two category averages. It helps explain why a softer housing market can feel quite different to a first-time condo buyer and a family looking for a detached house. Falling prices do not necessarily bring the next housing type within reach.

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board’s August Market Watch report put the overall average price 2.7% below a year earlier. The median sale price was lower still, at $850,000. The median marks the middle of the month’s transactions; expensive sales can pull the average upward. Neither figure describes the price of a particular home.

Average and median describe different aspects of the same month’s transactions. Both are affected by the mix of homes sold.

The steps between housing types

Between apartments and detached houses, August’s average prices were $681,447 for condo townhouses, $882,060 for attached and row townhouses, and $931,665 for semi-detached homes. The distinction between the two townhouse categories matters: grouping them together conceals a $200,613 difference in their average selling prices.

TRREB’s price-band table makes the difference more concrete. There were 1,058 condo apartment sales below $700,000 in August, compared with 182 detached sales below that threshold. Lower-priced houses did sell, but the completed transactions at that budget were much more concentrated in apartments. The comparison is useful for setting a search budget before narrowing it to a neighbourhood and a suitable home.

These are averages of different homes in different locations. They do not tell us what a buyer would pay for an extra bedroom, a backyard, or a change in ownership structure on the same street. They do show why a broad claim that townhouses are becoming affordable needs a more precise definition of the product and the buyer.

A household comparing a condo townhouse with a freehold alternative also has to compare the costs of ownership. The purchase price alone leaves out condominium fees, maintenance obligations and property-specific expenses. A lower selling price can make the down payment easier to assemble without producing an equivalent reduction in monthly costs.

Category averages compare different homes and locations; the gaps are not estimates of the cost to upgrade an otherwise identical property.

Lower prices do not determine what sells

Detached homes accounted for 2,399 of August’s 5,057 sales, or 47.4%. Condo apartments recorded 1,330 sales, or 26.3%. Semi-detached homes, attached and row townhouses, and condo townhouses each recorded fewer than 440 sales.

The most expensive major category still produced the most transactions. That does not establish that buyers prefer detached homes at any price. The number and location of existing homes, the properties offered for sale and the budgets of active buyers all shape the result. Sales counts are completed transactions, not a survey of what households would choose if money were no object.

For developers, that is a reason to be specific about a target purchaser. A project’s unit count cannot be justified simply by pointing to a large pool of households that need housing. Its price and layout have to fit the households able and willing to buy it. The resale record offers one check on those assumptions.

The five categories shown account for 5,000 of the board’s 5,057 sales. The remaining 57 transactions were in other housing categories.

Apartments still offer considerable choice

There were 7,882 condo apartments listed for sale across TRREB’s coverage area at the end of August. Apartments represented 32.2% of all active listings, compared with their 26.3% share of the month’s sales.

Those shares describe a larger concentration of apartments among available listings than among completed deals. They do not measure the chance that an individual listing will sell. Active listings are a count at month-end; sales cover the month, and properties enter and leave the market throughout it.

The practical implication for a new condominium project is the range of existing apartments its buyers can inspect. A new unit can offer features an older building lacks. Its premium still needs to make sense beside the size, location, condition and carrying costs of the available resale alternatives. August’s regional average cannot settle that comparison.

Monthly observations are not seasonally adjusted. Active listings count properties available at month-end; they are not construction inventory.

Even a detached-house average needs context

Within the City of Toronto, detached homes sold for an average of $1,525,749 in August. The median was $1,170,000, a difference of $355,749. That is a substantial gap within one housing type and one municipality.

A family using the average alone could overestimate what the middle of that month’s detached market cost. A developer using it as a comparable could make the opposite mistake: assuming an ordinary infill home competes directly with the expensive transactions that pull up the average.

The median is useful context, but it is also affected by which homes sell. Neither measure controls for lot size, neighbourhood or renovation quality. Those details become more important as the comparison moves from a regional report to a particular purchase or project.

Average and median prices share one dollar axis. These unadjusted transaction measures do not control for changes in the homes sold.

The condo comparison changes outside Toronto

Toronto condo apartments averaged $651,648, compared with $549,868 in the report’s 905 category. The $101,780 difference is a price gap between the apartments that sold in those two areas, not the measured cost of moving an identical unit across the city boundary.

For a buyer able to change location, it is a reason to widen the search and compare actual listings. For a project being priced outside Toronto, it is a reason to test assumptions against nearby resales before borrowing a city-wide price expectation.

Market Watch records resales. It does not tell us how many new units developers presold, whether a project can obtain financing or what it will cost to build. Its value to that industry is more immediate: it shows the prices buyers accepted for existing homes. August’s figures give developers a demanding set of comparisons, and buyers a clearer starting point than the GTA’s sub-$1-million headline.

TRREB’s 416/905 categories compare the apartments sold in each area. The difference does not isolate a location premium for equivalent units.

Source: TRREB Market Watch, August 2026. Charts: homiesai.com/stats. Historical charts use each month's stored Market Watch observations, captured for this edition; year-over-year comparisons use the revised figures in the latest report. All charts are not seasonally adjusted.

items.description: Five specialists in housing economics, regulation, and lending will determine this year's winners
items.content: <p>Five specialists in housing economics, regulation, and lending will determine this year's winners</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639246263011580058.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Five specialists in housing economics, regulation, and lending will determine this year's winners
items.body:
The judges who will determine Canada's top mortgage honours this November have been confirmed, bringing credentials that span academic research, regulatory law, federal housing policy, and 25 years of industry leadership.

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMA) are scheduled for November 25 at Rebel Toronto, marking the programme's 20th anniversary.

The ceremony spans 26 categories judged through a five-stage process, and the judging panel sits at the centre of a methodology designed to make the outcome as defensible as it is distinguished. 

A panel built on independence

All judges are required to sign a non-disclosure agreement to prevent the unauthorised disclosure of confidential information, including details within submission forms.

Any judge with a conflict of interest in a category is required to recuse themselves from voting in that category. 

The five confirmed judges bring expertise across disciplines that touch nearly every corner of the Canadian mortgage market.

Dr. Kiana Basiri, Assistant Professor at the Ted Rogers School of Management at Toronto Metropolitan University, brings an academic lens grounded in applied economics.

Her research focuses on using econometrics tools to understand the relationship between housing and credit markets, with a focus on real estate economics, housing policy, household finance, consumer bankruptcies, and default. She previously served as a Senior Specialist at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

Samantha Gale, Chief Executive Officer of Veracite Trust Company Ltd. and the Canadian Private Lenders Association (CPLA), arrives with 15 years of frontline regulatory experience.

A former CEO of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association – British Columbia and the Mortgage Brokers Institute of BC, she holds a Master of Laws from Osgoode Hall Law School specialising in banking and financial law and played a prominent role in the Cullen Commission.

Much of her expertise stems from her 15-year tenure with the BC Financial Institutions Commission (FICOM, now the BC Financial Services Authority, or BCFSA). 

Andrey Pavlov, Professor of Finance at the Beedie School of Business at Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, contributes a research profile that cuts across risk management, mortgage securitization, and financial derivatives.

He has consulted for organisations including Fannie Mae in the United States, Canada's federal government, the Government of British Columbia, and CMHC, and has served on the editorial boards of Real Estate Economics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics. 

Caroline Sanfaçon, Senior Vice-President of Insurance and Securitization at CMHC, brings more than two decades of direct experience in Canada's federal housing agency.

She leads the delivery of CMHC's commercial products, including mortgage loan insurance and securitization, with extensive experience in retail and commercial real estate credit risk and lending, and prior experience in CMHC offices in Montréal, Ottawa, and Vancouver. 

Rounding out the panel is Steven Ranson, the retired President and Chief Executive Officer of HomeEquity Bank, who spent almost 25 years leading the institution and helped transform reverse mortgages from a largely unknown product into a trusted financial tool for older Canadians.

He is the co-author of HomeRun: The Reverse Mortgage Advantage. 

How the winners are chosen

The judging panel is the final stage in a five-step process that begins well before the November gala. Nominations were open from June 8 to August 14 at 11:59 p.m. ET, and were open to all mortgage professionals and organisations across Canada, including brokers, brokerages, lenders, business development managers (BDMs), underwriters, agents, and service providers. There was no fee to submit a nomination. 

Following the close of nominations, the CMA team conducts its own research, drawing on knowledge gained through Canadian Mortgage Professional magazine, to ensure no deserving candidate is missed.

Excellence awardees — the final shortlist in each category — will be officially announced in September.

Judging is set to commence in October and November, with winners determined by a points-based system that aggregates each judge's votes.

The methodology is built specifically to guard against the risk of strong networks simply outrunning strong performance. 

For practitioners, recognition carries tangible professional value beyond the gala night itself.

Excellence awardees and winners will be announced in CMP magazine and online channels, profiled in online content, and featured in industry events throughout the year. 

The 2026 edition also expands the category roster, with new classifications reflecting how the broker's role continues to evolve. Two additions — Mortgage Tech Innovator of the Year and The REMIC Award for Finfluencer of the Year — signal that the industry's definition of excellence is broadening.

Full details on all 26 categories and how to get involved are available at canadianmortgageawards.com.

items.title: Interior B.C. real estate slows amid wildfire disruption
items.description: Kamloops saw milder year-over-year decline in home sales than broader interior region
items._ogDesc: Kamloops saw milder year-over-year decline in home sales than broader interior region
items.body:
Real estate activity across much of B.C.’s Interior slowed in August amid widespread wildfire disruption, according to a recent industry report.

The Association of Interior Realtors recorded 1,141 residential sales across its region in August, down from 1,496 in July and 13.4 per cent from the same month last year.

The association represents realtor members across much of B.C.’s Interior, including Kamloops, the Okanagan, Kootenay, Shuswap-Revelstoke and South Peace River.

“August was a difficult month for our communities,” Ryan Mayne, president of the Association of Interior Realtors, said in a news release last week. He noted that the association believes the decline in sales was related to wildfires across the region.

“Evacuations displaced families, homes were lost, and the focus rightfully shifted away from real estate … activity slowed as a result, which is completely understandable given what so many people were going through,” Mayne said.

There were 2,062 new residential listings recorded across the region in August, down 17.9 per cent from a year earlier and from 2,569 new listings in July, according to the association.

Active listings totalled 9,378 in August, down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year and slightly below July’s 9,630 listings.

Kamloops and the surrounding Thompson-Nicola region saw a milder decline in sales compared with the broader region, according to association.

The Kamloops and District market recorded 217 residential sales in August, a 14.5 per cent decrease from July and 1.4 per cent decrease from August 2025. Active listings in this market totalled 1,405, down 5.3 per cent year over year.

“Considering the wildfire and smoke conditions experienced across the province, the Kamloops and District market held up relatively well in August, with sales closely reflecting last year’s activity,” Mayne said.

“While listing levels continue to be more restrained than elsewhere in the Interior, the relationship between available inventory and demand remains balanced.”

The benchmark price for a single-family home in Kamloops and District was $669,100 in August, up 0.9 per cent from a year earlier, according to the association.

The benchmark price for townhomes fell 2.5 per cent year over year to $508,400, and declined 1.1 per cent to $375,900 for condos.

The post Canadian Rents Continue To Slide—Except In Atlantic Provinces appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian apartment rents fell in Q2 2026 led by drops in Alberta, but surging prices across Atlantic Canada are defying the national trend.
items.body:
Canada’s East-West divide is extending to rental affordability, and not in the way many would expect. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows national two-bedroom asking rents sliding further in Q2 2026, but Atlantic Canada defied the trend. The East Coast has seen rents surge, with Halifax now among the most expensive cities in the country. Out West, the market is moving in the opposite direction, with Alberta’s asking rents tumbling below what existing tenants are paying.

Canada’s Asking Rents Slide, But Most Expensive Markets Remain Detached From Reality

The national asking rent for a 2-bedroom unit fell 0.9% (-$20) to $2,130/month in Q2 2026, 3.6% ($80) lower than last year. However, it’ll set you back considerably more in the country’s most expensive CMAs. The monthly rent in Vancouver ($3,030) remains the highest in the country, roughly 42% higher than the average. It was followed by Toronto ($2,650), and Victoria ($2,640).

The ranking of the top 3 most expensive markets is unlikely to surprise anyone paying attention. However, fast growth in “spillover markets” is narrowing the gap.

Canada’s Formerly Affordable Cities Lead The Way Higher

The fastest-growing rents weren’t in the most expensive markets, but secondary and tertiary ones. The fastest annual growth in Q2 was observed in Thunder Bay (+6.5%), Sherbrooke (+5.7%), Halifax (+5.3%), and Saskatoon (+5.2%). Since the pandemic, these regions have been the recipients of young adults fleeing pricey cities for affordability. Persistent high growth is now starting to soften the primary reason these cities have attracted young adults—cheap rents.

Halifax is the best example of a city that may have just eliminated its main attraction. The average asking rent in the city rerached $2,400/month in Q2 2026, making it the 4th most expensive CMA for renters. It’s not just Halifax—it’s a trend that’s persisting right across Eastern Canada. Asking rents in Halifax now surpass nearly every major market outside of Vancouver, Toronto, and Victoria.

Western Canada Leads The Way For Lower Rents

While Eastern Canada is seeing rents soar, Western Canada generally led the decline in asking rents, with Montreal being the exception thrown into the mix. The largest annual drops in Q2 were in Abbotsford-Mission (-6.4%), Calgary (-6.4%), Montreal (-5.2%), and Vancouver (-4.1%). A good reminder that rents and incomes aren’t moving together in Canada’s big cities.

These sharp declines have created an unusual dynamic in Canada’s Prairies—asking rents are lower than existing ones. For example, in Calgary the asking rent of $1,890/month has slipped below the average rent paid by tenants ($1,930). Regina also saw its asking rent ($1,480) fall below paid rents ($1,580), while Edmonton’s asking and paid rents were both roughly equal at $1,570.

It’s easy to assume the East-West divergence is due to local economic strength, but it isn’t. Western Canada’s provinces have generally been reporting lower unemployment rates, and Alberta is the biggest recipient of interprovincial migration. Two major cities in Alberta are seeing rents plunge, but the province’s GDP growth is currently outpacing the much smaller provincial economies in Eastern Canada.

The soaring prices in Atlantic Canada are actually more characteristic of late-stage business growth. This is when excess credit can’t be efficiently allocated into productive resources, resulting in a concentration of asset financialization. As a result, property values surge, and the rents to use that land rise alongside servicing costs. Prices then move outward from the center in a process called “bubble contagion,” a trend that both Toronto and Vancouver became all too familiar with in recent years.
